title: Changes in Interpersonal Predictive Coding illustrated by the “Bayesian Ghost” Misperception in healthy Participants
summary:
The study investigates differences in social perception among healthy participants. A difference is made between participants who have previously engaged in a social interaction and those who have not. For interpreting complex situations within social interactions, prior assumptions and expectations—referred to as predictive coding—play an important role.
In addition to various tests, questionnaires, and motion tracking, the study employs the Bayesian Ghost paradigm. This is a computer-based task in which moving dots sometimes create the visual impression of human figures and sometimes do not. We specifically examine how participants interpret complex social situations based on their expectations and prior assumptions, a process described as predictive coding.
We expect that participants whose “social brain” has been pre-activated through interactive pantomime will show a greater tendency to falsely interpret social cues, leading to more Bayesian Ghost errors in the experimental group.
Furthermore, tests are conducted to assess attention, facial affect recognition, intelligence, loneliness, and other self-report measures of depressive symptoms.
Motion tracking is also used to measure the degree of synchronization between the movements of the participant and the experimenter. The estimated body posture is recorded using the Kinect software’s skeletal model. The data collected include only the positions of predefined body joints and basic facial information (e.g., gaze direction, whether the eyes are open or closed). Here, too, we hypothesize that participants who show a high degree of movement synchronization with the experimenter will make more Bayesian Ghost errors.
conditions: Only healthy participants are included in the study. The study aims to examine whether participants’ perception of stimuli can be influenced by the type of pantomime task they perform prior to the main experiment—specifically, whether they engage in socially interactive pantomime tasks with the experimenter or perform solo pantomime tasks. We hypothesize that activating the social brain through interactive pantomime increases the tendency to mistakenly rely on social cues, leading to a higher number of “Bayesian Ghost” errors in the experimental group. Furthermore, we expect that participants who show a higher degree of movement synchronization with the experimenter will also exhibit more “Bayesian Ghost” errors, reflected in a positive correlation. By addressing this research question, we aim to gain a deeper understanding of how social interaction influences perception. Such insights may, in the future, contribute to therapeutic applications in various psychological disorders (e.g., body dysmorphia and related conditions).

interventions.name:
Verum- group: 
Before the Bayesian Ghost paradigm, participants perform socially interactive pantomime tasks (five different tasks, each repeated four times; total duration approximately 20 minutes).

control group: 
Before the Bayesian Ghost paradigm, participants perform solo pantomime tasks (five different tasks, each repeated four times; total duration approximately 20 minutes).

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Sufficient knowledge of German (since the normative values of the psychometric tests are based on German-speaking participants, including participants with insufficient German skills would lead to a relevant distortion of the results; moreover, the informed consent documents are only available in German, and the experimenters have only sufficient German language proficiency)
Exclusion criteria:
- History of regular (>5 days per week) and heavy alcohol consumption (>60 g alcohol/day)
- History of cannabis, cocaine, amphetamine, heroin, or other substance use (excluding nicotine) within the past month
- Insufficient knowledge of the German language (see above)
- current psychiatric disorders, except for nicotine dependence
- Neurological disorders of the central nervous system
- Verbal IQ below 70
